mcqs.question: A product requires under 20ms p99 latency worldwide, served from a single US datacenter. Why can't better application code alone meet this for a user in another continent?
options: Because application code is never the bottleneck in any system
Because 20ms is technically impossible for any system to ever achieve
Because the database needs to be rewritten in a faster programming language
Because the physical round-trip time imposed by the speed of light in fiber over that distance already exceeds 20ms, regardless of how fast the server responds
mcqs.explanation: Cross-continental round trips take tens of milliseconds purely from physical distance and the speed of light in fiber - a floor no server-side optimization can remove. 20ms is achievable regionally, and language choice doesn't address a network-distance problem.

mcqs.question: A team notices their cloud bill for data leaving the provider's network (egress) is a major cost driver for a video-streaming feature. What is the most direct lever to address this?
options: Switch the backend programming language
Increase the number of app servers
Move all data into archive/cold storage
Serve the video from a CDN edge or keep traffic within a region to avoid repeated cross-network egress charges
mcqs.explanation: Egress cost is driven by data crossing network boundaries repeatedly; a CDN edge or regional locality directly reduces that. Programming language and app server count don't affect network egress, and archive storage would actually hurt a frequently-accessed video workload's latency and cost profile.

mcqs.question: A small team compares self-hosting a message queue ($200/month in raw infrastructure) against a managed equivalent ($600/month). Why might the managed option still be cheaper overall?
options: Managed services are always cheaper on the infrastructure line item too
The total cost comparison should include engineer time spent operating, patching, and handling failovers for the self-hosted option, which can easily exceed the price difference
Self-hosted systems never require any ongoing maintenance
It wouldn't be cheaper - the lower infrastructure number is always the correct comparison
mcqs.explanation: The fair comparison is total cost of ownership, including engineer-hours spent operating the self-hosted system - for a team without deep expertise in that system, this can dwarf the raw infra savings. The infra line item alone is misleading, and self-hosted systems do require real ongoing operational work.

mcqs.question: A team adds a new regional replica to fix latency complaints, but doesn't estimate the added cross-region replication and egress cost before doing so. What is the actual mistake described in the pitfall?
options: Adding a regional replica is always the wrong fix for latency complaints
Fixing the latency symptom without pricing the new cost it introduces means the trade-off was never made as an actual informed decision
Regions should never be added for any reason
The mistake is technical, not financial - the replica will not actually reduce latency
mcqs.explanation: The replica likely does help latency - the failure is treating that as the end of the analysis, when it also creates real, ongoing replication and egress costs that were never estimated or weighed. The pitfall isn't that adding a region is wrong in general, and it isn't a claim that the fix fails technically.

mcqs.question: A product requires a 30ms p99 response time for users across US, Europe, and Asia, served from a single US region. What does the reference table of round-trip floors tell you?
options: This is achievable with sufficiently optimized application code
Intercontinental round trips alone typically run 70-200ms, well above 30ms — this is fundamentally a geography problem, not something better code can fix
30ms is only a floor for same-datacenter calls, so it's irrelevant here
The requirement is realistic as long as caching is used aggressively
mcqs.explanation: The reference floors show intercontinental round trips already exceed 30ms before any processing happens, so no application-level optimization can close that gap — the fix has to be moving computation or data closer to users. Caching helps for repeated reads but doesn't change the physical round-trip floor for the request that has to cross that distance in the first place.

mcqs.question: Why is translating a proposed latency improvement into an estimated revenue figure a stronger argument for a multi-region investment than describing it purely in milliseconds?
options: It lets the decision be compared directly against the new region's cost using the same unit (money), rather than comparing a UX improvement against a dollar figure
Milliseconds are never meaningful to any stakeholder
Revenue estimates are always more accurate than latency measurements
This conversion is only relevant for e-commerce companies
mcqs.explanation: Converting latency into a rough revenue estimate puts both sides of the trade-off (cost of the new region vs. value of the latency fix) in the same unit, making the decision an apples-to-apples comparison instead of comparing an engineering metric against a budget line. It's not that milliseconds are meaningless, revenue estimates are rough approximations rather than guaranteed-accurate, and the general technique applies to any latency-sensitive product, not only e-commerce.
